edges.effect_quant: Across randomized evidence, introducing peanut in infancy substantially lowers later peanut allergy risk. A 2023 meta-analysis found a pooled RR of 0.31 for peanut introduction between 3 and 10 months, and the LEAP program showed durable protection through childhood and adolescence.
edges.population: infants, especially those at elevated allergy risk because of severe eczema, egg allergy, or other atopic features
edges.mechanism: Regular peanut exposure during an early immunologic window appears to promote oral tolerance rather than sensitization. Avoidance during infancy may leave high-risk children more vulnerable to developing persistent IgE-mediated peanut allergy.
edges.summary: This is one of the clearest prevention edges in pediatrics. Randomized trials and long-term follow-up consistently show that introducing peanut during infancy, rather than delaying it, markedly reduces later peanut allergy, with benefits persisting after periods of avoidance and into adolescence.
edges.caveats: Most of the strongest evidence comes from high-risk infants and from carefully structured introduction protocols, so implementation still depends on age-appropriate forms and clinical judgment for infants with severe eczema or suspected existing allergy. The effect is strongest for true regular ingestion rather than one-time exposure.

evidence.citation: Scarpone R et al 2023 JAMA Pediatr
evidence.notes: Timing of Allergenic Food Introduction and Risk of Immunoglobulin E-Mediated Food Allergy: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.

effect_quant.comparator: peanut allergy after peanut introduction between 3 and 10 months versus later introduction or avoidance

evidence.citation: DuToit G et al 2015 N Engl J Med
evidence.notes: Randomized trial of peanut consumption in infants at risk for peanut allergy.

effect_quant.comparator: peanut allergy prevalence at 60 months in the negative skin-prick-test intention-to-treat population: 1.9% with consumption versus 13.7% with avoidance

evidence.citation: DuToit G et al 2016 N Engl J Med
evidence.notes: Effect of Avoidance on Peanut Allergy after Early Peanut Consumption.

effect_quant.comparator: peanut allergy prevalence at 72 months after 12 months of avoidance: 4.8% in the original consumption group versus 18.6% in the original avoidance group

evidence.citation: DuToit G et al 2024 NEJM Evid
evidence.notes: Follow-up to Adolescence after Early Peanut Introduction for Allergy Prevention.

effect_quant.comparator: peanut allergy prevalence at age 144 months: 4.4% in the original consumption group versus 15.4% in the original avoidance group
